Is Java compiled or interpreted? Why is it called platform independent?

Both. javac compiles source into bytecode. The JVM then interprets that bytecode and JIT-compiles hot code to native machine code at runtime. The bytecode is the same everywhere, and each OS and CPU has its own JVM, so the same .class file runs on all of them. The JVM is platform-dependent; the bytecode is not. Portability can still break through native libraries, hard-coded file paths or a default charset assumption.
Walk through what happens when you run java com.shop.Hello.

- The OS starts the JVM, which reads its options and sets up memory.
- The launcher asks the application class loader for com.shop.Hello. Loading is delegated upward (bootstrap, platform, application), and the class file is found on the classpath.
- Linking: bytecode is verified, static fields get memory and default values, and symbolic references are resolved, usually lazily.
- The launcher looks up main. If it is missing, it prints an error, and the static initializer never runs. (A class with only a static { } block printed just the error on Java 21.)
- Initialization: parent static initializers run first, then the class's own.
- main runs on the main thread, first interpreted, then JIT-compiled where hot.
- The JVM exits when all non-daemon threads end or when System.exit is called.
Why is main public static void? Can it be overloaded, final, or in an interface?

Before Java 25: public so the launcher can access it, static so no instance is needed, and void because exit codes use System.exit. It can be overloaded, but only the standard form is the entry point. It can be final or synchronized, written with String..., inherited from a parent class, and placed in an interface, enum or record. Java 25 relaxes this: main may be non-public, an instance method, and parameterless (JEP 512). The return type must still be void.
Can a Java program run without a main method?

Before Java 7 a static block could run first and then call System.exit. Since Java 7 the launcher checks for main first, so that trick fails with "Main method not found". Environments where another program is the entry point are different: a servlet container or JUnit calls your code, but they have their own main. In Java 25 the method can be a simple void main(), but a main method is still required.
Can one source file have several classes? What does javac produce?

Yes. It may have any number of top-level types, but at most one public one, and the file must be named after it. javac writes a separate .class for each type, including Outer$Inner.class and Outer$1.class for nested and anonymous classes. Top-level classes can only be public or package-private; private, protected and static are compile errors there.
Does import java.util.* slow a program down or load all classes?

No. Imports exist only during compilation, as shorthand for names. The class file holds fully qualified names, and classes load lazily on first use. Compile time rises very slightly. Teams prefer explicit imports for readability and to avoid conflicts, such as Date in both java.util and java.sql, not for performance.
What are the default values? Why does int x; x++; fail while a field compiles?

Fields and array elements get zero-like defaults (0, 0.0, false, '\u0000', null) because the JVM zeroes heap memory when allocating. Locals live in stack frames, which are not cleared for speed. The language requires definite assignment instead: the compiler proves every path assigns the local before reading it, which turns a class of bugs into compile errors.
What is the size of a boolean?

The language specifies only the values, not a size. The JVM spec has no dedicated boolean arithmetic instructions: locals and stack values are handled as int, and boolean arrays use byte-sized instructions, so HotSpot uses one byte per element. Fields typically take one byte too. For a million flags, BitSet uses far less memory than boolean[].
Output? System.out.println((byte) 200); System.out.println((int) 3.99); System.out.println((int) Double.NaN); System.out.println((int) 1e20);

-56
3
0
2147483647
Integer narrowing keeps the low 8 bits: 200 is 1100 1000, and with the top bit as a sign that is -56. Floating to integer truncates toward zero, turns NaN into 0, and clamps out-of-range values to the limits.
Why does byte b = 10; b = b + 1; fail but b += 1; and b++; compile?

b + 1 is an int by numeric promotion, and assigning int to byte needs a cast because b is not a constant. b += 1 is defined as b = (byte)(b + 1), with the cast built in, and b++ behaves the same. Neither detects overflow, so byte b = 127; b++; gives -128.
Which of these compile? float f = 1.5; long l = 3000000000; Long w = 1; Byte b = 1; char c = -1; short s = 'a';

- float f = 1.5; no: a decimal literal is a double. Write 1.5f.
- long l = 3000000000; no: the literal itself is an int that is too large, so it needs L.
- Long w = 1; no: an int can box only to Integer, and Integer is not a Long.
- Byte b = 1; yes: constant narrowing followed by boxing is specifically allowed.
- char c = -1; no: -1 is outside char's range.
- short s = 'a'; yes: a constant that fits. With a non-constant char variable it fails.
Output? long a = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000; System.out.println(a);

500654080. All operands are int, so the product overflows before widening to long. The fix is to make the first operand long: 24L * 60 * ... gives 86400000000. In practice use Duration.ofDays(1).toMillis() and Math.multiplyExact.
Why is Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) negative? Where does this cause real bugs?

The range is -231 to 231-1, so +231 does not exist. Negating MIN_VALUE overflows back to itself. The usual bug is Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % buckets producing a negative index. Some strings do hash to exactly MIN_VALUE: "polygenelubricants" is the famous one. Use Math.floorMod(hash, buckets) or (hash & 0x7fffffff) % buckets.
Why is 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3? Does float behave differently?

0.1 and 0.2 have infinite binary expansions, so each is stored rounded. Their rounded sum is 0.30000000000000004, while the literal 0.3 rounds to a different double. float has the same limitation at lower precision, and the errors happen to cancel in print: 0.1f + 0.2f displays 0.3, which is luck. Compare with a tolerance, or use BigDecimal for exact decimal values.
What does 1/0, 1.0/0, 0.0/0 and 1%0 give?

1/0 and 1%0 throw ArithmeticException: / by zero, because integers have no value to represent the result. 1.0/0 gives Infinity and 0.0/0 gives NaN, because IEEE 754 defines those values. Floating-point arithmetic never throws.
How would you handle money in Java? Show the mistakes to avoid.

- Do not use double: rounding errors accumulate and totals stop matching.
- Use BigDecimal built from a String, or long minor units such as cents. new BigDecimal(0.1) captures the binary error.
- Choose a rounding mode and scale explicitly, as an accounting decision. divide without one throws on non-terminating results such as 1/3.
- Compare with compareTo, because equals says 2.0 and 2.00 differ.
- Store as a SQL DECIMAL, and keep the currency beside the amount.
- Allocate carefully: splitting 100.00 among 3 gives 33.33 three times, which loses a cent. Assign the remainder explicitly.
Math.round(2.5), Math.round(-2.5), Math.rint(2.5)?
3, -2 and 2.0. Math.round rounds ties toward positive infinity, as if by floor(x + 0.5), so -2.5 goes to -2, not -3. rint rounds ties to the even neighbour and returns a double.
Output of these Integer comparisons, and why?
int or Integer for a field in an entity or DTO?

Use int where a value is mandatory and always present, such as a counter. Use Integer or Long where absent is meaningful: a nullable column, an optional JSON field, or a generated ID. With a primitive, a missing value silently becomes 0, which you cannot distinguish from a real 0. JPA also treats a null ID as "new entity", which is why entity IDs are usually Long. The cost of wrappers is memory, unboxing NPEs, and the == trap.
Why can this line throw NPE: Integer r = flag ? 1 : map.get("k");?

One branch is int and the other Integer, so the ternary's type is int. When flag is false and the map has no key, null gets unboxed before the assignment. Fix it with if/else, or make both branches Integer: flag ? Integer.valueOf(1) : map.get("k").

88
1.0
When one branch is char and the other is an int constant that fits in char, the result is char. A non-constant int variable forces promotion to int, so 'X' prints as 88. In the third, int and double give double.

char values promote to int under + unless a String is already on the left. + is left-associative, so the type at each step decides.
Why does int i = 5; i = i++; leave i at 5? Answer at bytecode level.

Bytecode from javac: iload_0 pushes 5, iinc updates the local to 6, and istore_0 writes the pushed 5 back. The right side computes its value before the assignment, and the increment finishes inside the right side. Plain i++; as a statement is the correct way.
Output? int i = 5; int j = i++ + ++i; int k = 10; k += k++ + ++k;

j is 12 and i is 7: the operands are 5 (i becomes 6), then 7. k is 32. The compound assignment saves the left value 10 first, then evaluates 10 + 12, and stores 10 + 22. Java evaluates left to right, so this is defined behaviour, unlike the same expression in C. Do not write it in real code.

1

An int shift uses only the low 5 bits of the distance, so 32 acts as 0, while long uses 6 bits. >>> fills with zeros, leaving 4 set bits. >> copies the sign bit, so -1 stays -1.
What is the difference between & and &&?

&& works only on booleans and short-circuits. & on booleans always evaluates both sides, and on integers it is bitwise AND. obj != null & obj.isOk() throws NPE when obj is null. Note that & and | are precedence-lower than ==, so bit tests need parentheses.
Check whether a number is a power of two, odd, and count its set bits, without loops over digits.
How do you swap two ints without a temporary? Should you?

a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b;   // works even with overflow, thanks to wrap-around
a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;            // XOR version
a = (b + (b = a)) - b;             // obfuscated, relies on left-to-right order
Either breaks if both are the same array slot, for example arr[i] and arr[j] with i == j: XOR zeroes it. A temporary is clearer, and the JIT produces code at least as good. Say that in the interview.
What is switch fall-through? Output of switch (2) { case 1: print("a"); case 2: print("b"); case 3: print("c"); break; default: print("d"); }?

bc. Execution jumps to the matching label and continues through later labels until a break. Fall-through is occasionally intentional, but it is a common source of bugs, which is why the arrow form has none.
Why can you not switch on a long? How does a String switch work?

The JVM switch instructions, tableswitch and lookupswitch, take 32-bit int keys. A String switch is compiled to a lookupswitch on hashCode(), followed by equals() to rule out collisions, which then sets a temporary index, followed by a second switch on that index. "Aa" and "BB" share a hash code and can both be cases without problem. A null string throws NPE at the hashCode() call. Java 21 adds case null.
yield vs return? Arrow vs colon?

yield supplies the value of the enclosing switch expression. return would leave the method, and is not allowed inside a switch expression. Arrow cases run just one expression, block or throw, with no fall-through. Colon cases keep fall-through, even in a switch expression. You choose per switch, and cannot mix them.
Does this compile? switch (o) { case Object p -> ...; case String s -> ...; }

No. case String s can never match, so javac reports "this case label is dominated by a preceding case label". Order from most specific to most general. A guarded pattern does not dominate: case Integer i when i > 0 before case Integer i is valid.
Output? Nested loops with continue outer and break outer.
Are arrays objects? Where do they live? Why does a.length have no parentheses while s.length() does?

Yes. Even int[] extends Object, lives on the heap, and has a header containing the length. The length is read with the dedicated arraylength instruction, which the language presents as a final field. String.length() is an ordinary method. Arrays override clone to be public, and do not override equals, hashCode or toString, which is why printing one gives [I@1b6d3586-style text.
What does cloning a 2D array do? How do you deep-copy one?
Explain ArrayStoreException. Why are generics invariant when arrays are covariant?

Object[] o = new String[1]; o[0] = 1; compiles because String[] is an Object[], and fails at runtime because every array knows its element type and checks each store. Arrays need that check; generics are erased, so they cannot check at runtime. Making List<String> a subtype of List<Object> would allow heap corruption with no error, so generics are invariant, with wildcards (? extends T) for safe read-only covariance.
Which output? vs("a", (Object) null), vs("a", (Object[]) null), vs("a", new int[]{1, 2}), for String vs(String a, Object... r) returning r's length or "null".

1, null, 1. Casting to Object means one element which is null, so the compiler wraps it in an array. Casting to Object[] passes the array parameter directly, as null. An int[] is not an Object[], so it becomes a single element. A String[] would be spread, with its length used.
Why does a long overload beat Integer for an int argument?

Overload resolution runs three phases and stops at the first that yields a candidate: (1) subtyping and primitive widening, (2) boxing and unboxing, (3) var-args. long is reached in phase 1, Integer only in phase 2. The reason is backward compatibility: code written before Java 5 had to keep calling the same methods once boxing arrived.
Is Java pass-by-reference for objects? Prove it either way.

No, it is pass-by-value, and a reference value gets copied. Proof: reassigning a parameter inside a method never changes the caller's variable, and a swap(a, b) on two objects has no effect. In true pass-by-reference (C++ int&) it would. People get confused because mutation through the copied reference is visible to the caller. This matters in practice for String and wrappers: a method cannot "return through" an immutable parameter.
When is recursion a bad choice in Java? What is the depth limit?

There is no fixed limit; depth depends on stack size (-Xss) and frame size, and JIT-compiled frames differ from interpreted ones, so the depth varies from run to run. Typical defaults allow thousands to tens of thousands of simple frames. Avoid recursion when depth grows with input, such as walking a long linked list or a user-supplied JSON tree. Java does no tail-call optimization, so rewrite it as a loop, use an explicit stack, or at least enforce a depth limit. Catching StackOverflowError is not a design.
Print the order of execution for parent and child static blocks, instance blocks and constructors.

Parent statics, child statics (both once per class load), then for each object: parent fields and instance blocks, parent constructor, child fields and instance blocks, child constructor. Fields and blocks within a class run in source order. The important trap: a parent constructor calling an overridden method runs the child's version while child fields still hold defaults, so it printed name=null in the example above.
Output? Why is Cnt.b 0 while Cnt.a is 1?
Does reading Child.parentStaticField initialize Child?

No, only the class that declares the field is initialized. Reading a compile-time constant initializes neither, since the value was inlined, and creating new A[1] does not initialize A. All verified: in the example above, B.BOXED prints "A init" but never "B init".
Can a constructor be static or final? What is an instance initializer block for?

Neither. A constructor is not inherited, so final has no meaning, and it always works on a new instance, so static has none either; both are compile errors. Instance initializer blocks hold code shared by all constructors, and are required in anonymous classes, which cannot declare constructors. In practice a private init method or constructor chaining with this(...) reads better. A void T() method named after its class compiles, and is just an ordinary method. It is a known trick question.
What does final guarantee for a reference? Can a final field be set without a value at declaration?

It guarantees the variable keeps pointing to the same object. It does not freeze the object: final List<String> l can still be added to. A blank final can be set in an instance initializer or constructor, and must be assigned exactly once on every constructor path. A blank static final is set in a static block. Final fields also give a concurrency guarantee: a correctly constructed object's final fields are visible to other threads without synchronization.
Is var dynamic typing? Name places it cannot be used.

No. The type is inferred once, at compile time, and cannot change. var is not allowed on fields, method parameters, return types, or catch parameters, nor without an initializer, with null, with an array initializer, or with a lambda or method reference. It is allowed in local declarations, for loops, try-with-resources, and implicitly typed lambda parameters since Java 11, so you can attach annotations: (@NonNull var x) -> x.
Are goto, const, true, null and var keywords?

goto and const are reserved keywords with no meaning, kept so that nobody uses them and to give better errors. true, false and null are literals, and also unusable as identifiers. var, yield and record are contextual: int var = 1; and int record = 1; compile, but a class cannot be named var since Java 10.
A unit test passes with IDs 1 to 100 but production says two equal orders are different. Where do you look?

First suspect == on Long or Integer: identical values share a cached object only up to 127. Replace with equals or Objects.equals, or compare unboxed values. Also check equals between Long and Integer (always false), for example comparing an API-parsed Integer with a DB Long. Add a Sonar or Error Prone rule for reference equality on boxed types, and test with values above 127.
Output? Foo foo = null; System.out.println(foo.hi()); where hi is static.

It prints the method's result with no NPE. javac resolves a static call from the declared type, and the bytecode is invokestatic, which ignores the reference. The same applies to static fields. It is legal but misleading, and compilers warn about it.
Why does System.out.println(null) not compile, when m(null) works with m(Object) and m(String)?

null fits any reference parameter. With Object and String, String is more specific, so it wins. println has both println(char[]) and println(String), which are unrelated types, so neither is more specific: "reference to println is ambiguous". Casting (Object) null or (String) null resolves it.
Does this comment execute? // \u000a System.out.println("hi");

Yes, it prints hi. Unicode escapes are processed in the first step of lexing, before comments are recognized, so \u000a is a real newline and the rest of the line is code. For the same reason a \u000a inside a string literal is a compile error. Verified on Java 21.
What is wrong with this for-each? for (Integer x : list) if (x == 2) list.remove(x);

Normally it throws ConcurrentModificationException, because the hidden iterator detects the structural change on the next next(). With [1, 2, 3] it surprisingly does not throw and prints [1, 3]: after removing the second-to-last element, hasNext() compares cursor 2 with the new size 2 and stops, so the check never runs. Use list.removeIf(x -> x == 2) or an explicit iterator's remove().
Scanner reads a number, then an empty line appears instead of the name. Why?

nextInt() stops right after the digits and leaves the line terminator in the buffer. nextLine() then returns the empty remainder of that line. Consume it with one extra nextLine(), or read everything with nextLine() and call Integer.parseInt(line.trim()). The second handles bad input more cleanly too.
Random vs ThreadLocalRandom vs SecureRandom: which do you pick?

- Random: seedable, so use it when you need repeatable sequences, such as tests or simulations. Shared across threads it suffers from contention.
- ThreadLocalRandom.current(): the default for general concurrent server code, such as retry jitter.
- SecureRandom: anything an attacker must not predict, such as session IDs, reset tokens or salts.
How do you avoid NullPointerExceptions in a large codebase?

- Make invalid states impossible: require non-null constructor arguments with Objects.requireNonNull, so failures appear at the source rather than far away.
- Return empty collections and Optional, not null.
- Prefer constant-first comparison ("x".equals(s)) and Objects.equals.
- Watch hidden unboxing: ternaries, map.get, method parameters of type int.
- Validate at the edges with Bean Validation, and map nullable DB columns to wrappers deliberately.
- Use a nullness checker (for example JSpecify annotations with NullAway) in CI.
- Do not catch NPE as control flow.
Is Java a purely object-oriented language?

No. Java has primitive types (int, double, and so on) that are not objects, and static members that belong to no object. Smalltalk, by contrast, treats everything as an object. The primitives exist for performance. Wrappers and autoboxing let them take part in object APIs such as collections and generics. 💡 Project Valhalla (value classes) aims to narrow this gap, but it is not part of the Java 21 LTS.
Should you use assert to validate method arguments?

Not for public methods. Assertions are off unless the JVM runs with -ea, so a check that protects data or security would silently disappear in production. For public arguments, throw IllegalArgumentException, NullPointerException (through Objects.requireNonNull) or IllegalStateException, or use Bean Validation in Spring. assert is for internal invariants in private code, for example "this branch is unreachable" or "the array is sorted here". Never put a side effect inside an assert.
What do transient, volatile, native, synchronized and strictfp mean?

- transient (field): skipped by Java serialization. Jackson will not use the field directly, but a public getter is still serialized unless MapperFeature.PROPAGATE_TRANSIENT_MARKER is on, so use @JsonIgnore. For JPA, the explicit form is @Transient.
- volatile (field): reads and writes go to main memory and are ordered (happens-before), so other threads see changes. It gives visibility, not atomicity: count++ is still unsafe.
- native (method): the body is implemented in C or C++ through JNI, for example Object.hashCode.
- synchronized (method or block): mutual exclusion on a monitor, plus visibility.
- strictfp: obsolete. Since Java 17 (JEP 306), all floating-point math is strict, so the keyword has no effect.
How do you read an unsigned byte from a byte[] (for example, a file header)?

A byte is signed (-128 to 127), so (byte) 0xFF reads back as -1, and widening to int sign-extends it. Mask it with b & 0xFF, or use Byte.toUnsignedInt(b), to get 0 to 255. For multi-byte values, combine the masked bytes with shifts, or use ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes).order(ByteOrder.BIG_ENDIAN).getInt(). For 32-bit unsigned values, store them in a long using Integer.toUnsignedLong.
How do you compute "pages needed" (rounding up) with integer division?

Integer division truncates toward zero, so 101 / 10 is 10. Use (n + size - 1) / size for non-negative values. Be aware that n + size - 1 can overflow near Integer.MAX_VALUE. Since Java 18, Math.ceilDiv(n, size) handles this correctly, and Math.floorDiv is its counterpart. Avoid (int) Math.ceil(n / size): the division has already truncated before ceil runs. Math.ceil((double) n / size) works, but it goes through floating point.
for vs enhanced for vs while vs do-while: which loop fits?

| for | Enhanced for | while | do-while
Body runs at least once | No | No | No | Yes
Index available | Yes | No | If you keep one | If you keep one
Works on | Anything | Arrays and Iterable | Anything | Anything
Can remove from a list | Yes, carefully (index shifts) | No: list.remove usually throws ConcurrentModificationException | Yes, with an explicit Iterator | Rarely used for this
Typical use | Counted loops, two indexes | Read every element | Unknown number of steps | Read input, then check it
Rule of thumb: default to the enhanced for for reading, use an index loop when you need the position, and use while when the stop condition is not a count. For arrays, the enhanced for compiles to an index loop; for collections it uses an Iterator.
/ and % vs Math.floorDiv and Math.floorMod: what differs for negatives?

Expression | / and % | floorDiv and floorMod
Rounding | Toward zero | Toward negative infinity
-7, 2 | -7 / 2 = -3, -7 % 2 = -1 | floorDiv = -4, floorMod = 1
7, -2 | -3, 1 | -4, -1
Sign of remainder | Same as the dividend | Same as the divisor
int slot = Math.floorMod(hash, buckets);   // always 0..buckets-1
boolean odd = n % 2 != 0;                  // not n % 2 == 1, which fails for negatives
Rule of thumb: use floorMod for circular indexes, bucket numbers and day-of-week arithmetic, where a negative result is a bug. Both forms throw ArithmeticException on division by zero for integers.
== vs equals vs Arrays.equals vs Arrays.deepEquals on arrays?

| a == b | a.equals(b) | Arrays.equals(a, b) | Arrays.deepEquals(a, b)
Compares | References | References (inherited from Object) | Length and each element | Length and elements, recursing into nested arrays
int[]{1,2} vs int[]{1,2} | false | false | true | n/a (takes Object[])
int[][]{{1}} vs int[][]{{1}} | false | false | false (inner arrays compared by reference) | true
Matching hash | n/a | hashCode() (identity) | Arrays.hashCode | Arrays.deepHashCode
Interview tip: arrays never override equals, hashCode or toString. That is why an array is a poor HashMap key and why a record with an array component compares by reference. Use Arrays.toString or deepToString for printing.
Integer.parseInt vs Integer.valueOf vs new Integer: which do you call?

| parseInt(s) | valueOf(s) / valueOf(int) | new Integer(x)
Returns | int | Integer | Integer
Caching | n/a | Reuses objects for -128 to 127 | Always a new object
Bad input | NumberFormatException | NumberFormatException | NumberFormatException
Status | Normal | Normal; used by autoboxing | Deprecated since Java 9, marked for removal
Rule of thumb: use parseInt when you need a primitive, valueOf when you need an object, and never the constructor. Neither parse method trims spaces, so parseInt(" 5") throws.
